claim: Asthma has a strong genetic component with heritability estimated to be ~60–70%.
source: It has a strong genetic component, and twin studies estimate its heritability to be ~60–70% (Duffy et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to twin studies by Duffy et al., 1990

claim: The first asthma GWAS (2007) identified multiple markers on chromosome 17q21 associated with childhood onset asthma.
source: The first asthma GWAS (2007) identified multiple markers on chromosome 17q21 associated with childhood onset asthma (Moffatt et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moffatt et al., 2007

claim: The most widely replicated asthma locus is 17q12-21.
source: The most widely replicated locus is 17q12-21, followed by 6p21 (HLA region), 2q12 (IL1RL1/IL18R1), 5q22 (TSLP), and 9p24 (IL33) (Kim and Ober, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Ober, 2019

claim: Only a small proportion of asthma heritability is accounted for by identified genes.
source: However, despite undeniable successes, genetic studies of asthma have produced relatively heterogeneous results, and only a small proportion of the heritability is accounted for (Ober and Yao, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ober and Yao, 2011

claim: Most GWASs used a definition of 'doctor-diagnosed asthma' to maximize sample size.
source: However, in order to maximise sample size, most GWASs used a definition of 'doctor-diagnosed asthma' (Aaron et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aaron et al., 2017

claim: Aggregated asthma outcome definitions are imprecise and phenotypically heterogeneous.
source: Such aggregated outcome definitions are imprecise (Looijmans-van den Akker et al., 2016) and phenotypically and mechanistically heterogeneous (Robinson et al., 2021), and this heterogeneity may dilute important genetic signals (Custovic et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Looijmans-van den Akker et al., 2016, Robinson et al., 2021, and Custovic et al., 2019

claim: Five distinct wheezing phenotypes were identified by jointly modeling data from birth to adolescence in five UK birth cohorts.
source: For example, we jointly modelled data on wheezing from birth to adolescence in five UK population-based birth cohorts and identified five distinct phenotypes (Oksel et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oksel et al., 2019a

claim: The STELAR consortium brings together five UK population-based birth cohorts: ALSPAC, Ashford, IOW, MAAS, and SEATON.
source: The Study Team for Early Life Asthma Research (STELAR) consortium (Custovic et al., 2015) brings together five UK population-based birth cohorts: Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) (Golding et al., 2001), Ashford (Cullinan et al., 2004) and Isle of Wight (IOW) (Arshad et al., 2018) cohorts, Manchester Asthma and Allergy Study (MAAS) (Custovic et al., 2002), and the Aberdeen Study of Eczema and Asthma to Observe the Effects of Nutrition (SEATON) (Martindale et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple cohort studies

claim: A five-class solution was selected as the optimal model for wheeze phenotypes, labeled as: never/infrequent wheeze (52.4%), early-onset pre-school remitting wheeze (18.6%), early-onset middle-childhood remitting wheeze (9.8%), early-onset persistent wheeze (10.4%), and late-onset wheeze (8.8%).
source: A five-class solution was selected as the optimal model (Oksel et al., 2019a), and the classes (wheeze phenotypes) were labeled as: (1) never/infrequent wheeze (52.4%); (2) early-onset pre-school remitting wheeze (18.6%); (3) early-onset middle-childhood remitting wheeze (9.8%); (4) early-onset persistent wheeze (10.4%); and (5) late-onset wheeze (8.8%).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oksel et al., 2019a and data from the study

claim: The study included a total of 9568 subjects with European ancestry across five cohorts.
source: We included a total of 9568 subjects with European ancestry: ALSPAC, n=6833; MAAS, n=887; SEATON, n=548; Ashford, n=348; and IOW, n=952.
evidence: Directly stated sample sizes from the study

claim: A meta-analysis of three GWASs was performed using METAL with a total of 8,057,852 SNPs.
source: A meta-analysis of the three GWASs was performed using METAL (Willer et al., 2010) with a total of 8,057,852 SNPs.
evidence: Supported by citation to METAL software and data from the study

claim: Genomic inflation factor (λ) for early-onset pre-school remitting = 0.96, early-onset mid-childhood remitting = 0.94, late-onset = 0.96, and early-onset persistent wheezing = 0.97.
source: Genomic inflation factor (λ) for early-onset pre-school remitting = 0.96, early-onset mid-childhood remitting = 0.94, late-onset = 0.96, and early-onset persistent wheezing = 0.97.
evidence: Statistical measures from the GWAS analysis

claim: A total of 589 SNPs were associated with at least one phenotype with p<10–5.
source: A total of 589 SNPs were associated with at least one phenotype with p<10–5.
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis

claim: After clumping, 134 independent SNPs were identified uniquely associated with different phenotypes (p<10–5): 44 with early-onset persistent, 25 with early-onset pre-school remitting, 33 with early-onset mid-childhood remitting, and 32 with late-onset wheeze.
source: After clumping, we identified 134 independent SNPs uniquely associated with different phenotypes (p<10–5): of these, 44 were exclusively associated with early-onset persistent, 25 with early-onset pre-school remitting, 33 with early-onset mid-childhood remitting, and 32 with late-onset wheeze (Appendix 2—table 1).
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis after clumping procedure

claim: All genetic signals were phenotype-specific at p<10–5 and only nominal associations were shared across wheezing phenotypes.
source: The plots show that all signals were phenotype-specific at p<10–5 and only nominal associations were shared across wheezing phenotypes.
evidence: Interpretation of scatter plots showing heterogeneity in genetic profiles

claim: Chr17q21 was identified as a top locus for early-onset persistent wheeze (p=5.42 × 10–9).
source: For example, chr17q21 was identified as a top locus for early-onset persistent wheeze (p=5.42 × 10–9), but some of the SNPs in this region were also associated with the early-onset mid-childhood remitting phenotype (p<10–4).
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis

claim: Two GWAS-significant loci were identified for early-onset persistent wheeze: 17q21 (p<5.5 × 10–9) and a novel locus on 9q21.13 (ANXA1) (p<6.7 × 10–9).
source: We identified two GWAS-significant loci for early-onset persistent wheeze: 17q21, p<5.5 × 10–9, and a novel locus on 9q21.13 (ANXA1), p<6.7 × 10–9.
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis

claim: The ANXA1 locus was the only GWAS-significant locus that had not previously been associated with asthma or atopic traits.
source: The ANXA1 locus was the only GWAS-significant locus that had not previously been associated with asthma or atopic traits, with one previous study showing an association with FEV1/FVC and bronchodilator response in smokers (Lutz et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison with previous literature and citation to Lutz et al., 2015

claim: ANXA1 is strongly expressed in bronchial mast cells and has anti-inflammatory properties.
source: ANXA1 is strongly expressed in bronchial mast cells and has anti-inflammatory properties (Vieira Braga et al., 2019), and may be involved in epithelial airway repair (Leoni et al., 2015; Appendix 4—table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vieira Braga et al., 2019 and Leoni et al., 2015

claim: Two SNPs (rs75260654 and rs116849664) were associated with early-onset persistent wheeze at genome-wide significance.
source: Two SNPs (rs75260654, the lead SNP, and rs116849664 located downstream of ANXA1) were associated with early-onset persistent wheeze at genome-wide significance (GWS), with an additional SNP rs78320984 almost reaching GWS (Appendix 5—table 1).
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis

claim: Rs75260654, rs116849664, and rs78320984 are in linkage disequilibrium with each other but not with any other SNPs.
source: These SNPs are in linkage disequilibrium (LD) with each other (Appendix 5—figure 1), but not with any other SNPs.
evidence: Results from linkage disequilibrium analysis

claim: Rs75260654 overlapped a region interacting with the ANXA1 promoter in CD4+ cells.
source: Of the three SNPs, only rs75260654 overlapped a region interacting with the ANXA1 promoter (Figure 3).
evidence: Results from Promoter Capture Hi-C analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: Rs75260654 overlapped a POLR2A ChIP-seq peak and an ATAC-seq peak and active enhancer in the type II pneumocyte-derived A549 cell line.
source: Moreover, rs75260654 overlapped a POLR2A ChIP-seq peaks and an ATAC-seq peak and active enhancer in the type II pneumocyte-derived A549 cell line.
evidence: Results from ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq analyses

claim: Rs75260654 is located in a region directly interacting with the ANXA1 promoter and is transcriptionally active in relevant cell types.
source: This shows that rs75260654 is located in a region directly interacting with the ANXA1 promoter and is transcriptionally active in relevant cell types.
evidence: Inference from PCHi-C, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq data

claim: Two individuals were homozygote for the minor allele (T) of rs75260654, and both were in the early-onset persistent wheeze class.
source: Two individuals (one in MAAS and one in ALSPAC) were homozygote for the minor allele (T), and both were in the early-onset persistent wheeze class.
evidence: Genotype data from the study cohorts

claim: Rs75260654 (C changed to T) is located downstream of three protein-coding transcripts of AXNA1 and overlaps the known regulatory region ID ENSR00000882742 on Chromosome 9: 73,173,001–73,173,200.
source: Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) prediction shows the SNP rs75260654 (C changed to T) to be located downstream of three protein-coding transcripts of AXNA1 and overlapping the known regulatory region ID ENSR00000882742 on Chromosome 9: 73,173,001–73,173,200.
evidence: Results from Variant Effect Predictor analysis

claim: The T allele of rs75260654 reduces the expression of ANXA1 in naïve B cells (effect size = −2.36795, p=0.01).
source: Compared to C, the T allele was found to reduce the expression of ANXA1 in naïve B cells (effect size = −2.36795, p=0.01) and to increase expression in lymphoblasoid cell lines (effect size = 0.848856, pe = 0.001) (Figure 4).
evidence: Results from eQTL GTEX data shown in Figure 4

claim: The T allele of rs75260654 increases ANXA1 expression in lymphoblasoid cell lines (effect size = 0.848856, p = 0.001).
source: Compared to C, the T allele was found to reduce the expression of ANXA1 in naïve B cells (effect size = −2.36795, p=0.01) and to increase expression in lymphoblasoid cell lines (effect size = 0.848856, pe = 0.001) (Figure 4).
evidence: Results from eQTL GTEX data shown in Figure 4

claim: Rs75260654 affects expression of the neighbouring gene ALDH1A1 (effect size = −2.40446, p=0.0039 in macrophages infected with Salmonella).
source: This SNP affects expression of the neighbouring gene ALDH1A1 (aldehyde dehydrogenase-1 family member A1) (effect size = −2.40446, p=0.0039 in macrophages infected with Salmonella).
evidence: Results from eQTL analysis

claim: Rs75260654 is identified as an eQTL of ANXA1 in various immune cells including T cells, monocytes, fibroblasts, whole blood, Th2 memory cells, and naïve B cells at nominal significance.
source: In the eQTL catalogue, rs75260654 is identified as an eQTL of ANXA1 in various immune cells (at nominal significance) including T cells, monocytes, fibroblasts, whole blood, Th2 memory cells, naïve B cells.
evidence: Results from eQTL catalogue analysis

claim: Rs75260654 is an eQTL of ANXA1 in monocytes stimulated with R848 and human seasonal influenza A virus at nominal significance.
source: rs75260654 is also an eQTL of ANXA1 in monocytes that were stimulated with R848 (agonist of TLRs 7 and 8) and a human seasonal influenza A virus (Quach et al., 2016) (at nominal significance) (Appendix 5—table 3).
evidence: Results from eQTL analysis with citation to Quach et al., 2016

claim: Rs116849664 and rs78320984 (both in LD with rs75260654) were eQTLs of ANXA1 in the lung at nominal significance levels.
source: In the lung rs116849664 and rs78320984 (both in LD with rs75260654) were eQTLs of ANXA1 (Appendix 5—table 4) as well as LINC01474 at nominal significance levels.
evidence: Results from eQTL analysis in lung tissue

claim: eQTLGene Consortium meta-analysis showed a cis-eQTL effect of rs75260654 on ANXA1 (p=6.02 × 10–23) and ALDH1A1 (p=1.11 × 10–19) at FDR = 0.
source: Additional supporting evidence regarding the significance of the T-allele on the expression of these genes was provided using eQTLGene Consortium meta-analysis of 24 cohorts and 24,331 samples (Võsa et al., 2018). This method reproduced the previous modest results showing a cis-eQTL effect of rs75260654 on both the ANXA1 (p=6.02 × 10–23) and ALDH1A1 (p=1.11 × 10–19) at FDR = 0.
evidence: Results from eQTLGene Consortium meta-analysis with citation to Võsa et al., 2018

claim: ANXA1 interacts directly with genes enriched for asthma (including IL4 and IL13) and inflammatory regulation (NR3C1, glucocorticoid receptor).
source: Protein-protein network analysis demonstrated that ANXA1 interacts directly with genes enriched for asthma (including IL4 and IL13) and inflammatory regulation (NR3C1, glucocorticoid receptor) showing its significance in dysregulation of the immune response (see Appendix 5—figure 2 and Appendix 5—table 5).
evidence: Results from protein-protein network analysis

claim: Anxa1 protein expression increased following HDM challenge in a murine model.
source: Consistently, immunohistochemistry analysis revealed anxa1 protein expression increased following HDM challenge (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Results from immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 5B and C

claim: Anxa1 mRNA was significantly induced in lung tissue following HDM exposure.
source: Anxa1 mRNA was significantly induced in lung tissue following HDM exposure (Figure 5D).
evidence: Results from mRNA expression analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: Mice deficient in anxa1 had significantly worse lung function (greater airway resistance) compared to WT-treated mice.
source: Wildtype (WT) mice given HDM over 3 weeks developed significant airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) compared to PBS control mice. Mice deficient in anxa1 had significantly worse lung function (greater airway resistance) compared to WT-treated mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: Results from murine model experiments shown in Figure 5E

claim: Anxa1-/- mice exhibited significantly increased airway eosinophilia and elevated numbers of Th2 lymphocytes.
source: Anxa1-/- mice exhibited significantly increased airway eosinophilia and elevated numbers of Th2 lymphocytes (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Results from murine model experiments shown in Figure 5F and G

claim: Lung tissue cytokine levels in anxa1-/- mice showed elevation in IL-4 and significant induction of IL-5 and IL-13.
source: Lung tissue cytokine levels reflected the exacerbated airway Th2 inflammation, with elevation in IL-4, and significant induction of IL-5 and IL-13 (Figure 5H and J).
evidence: Results from ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5H and J

claim: Anxa1 deficiency results in an alteration of the pulmonary immune response, with uncontrolled eosinophilia and an exacerbation of type 2 inflammation and AHR in response to allergen.
source: Thus, anxa1 deficiency results in an alteration of the pulmonary immune response, with uncontrolled eosinophilia and an exacerbation of type 2 inflammation and AHR in response to allergen.
evidence: Inference from the murine model experimental results

claim: Each wheeze phenotype is characterized by unique phenotype-specific genetic associations with limited shared variants across phenotypes.
source: This suggests that genetic architecture of different wheeze phenotypes comprises a limited number of variants likely underpinning mechanisms which are shared across phenotypes, but that each phenotype is also characterised by unique phenotype-specific genetic associations.
evidence: Inference from the GWAS results showing phenotype-specific associations

claim: ANXA1 is a 37 kDa glycoprotein with potent anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving properties mediated by interaction with FPR2.
source: ANXA1 is a 37 kDa glycoprotein with potent anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving properties that are mediated by interaction with a specific G protein-coupled receptor FPR2 (Perretti et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perretti et al., 2002 and established scientific knowledge

claim: The ANXA1/FPR2 axis represents an important resolution pathway in chronic inflammatory settings such as rheumatoid arthritis and ulcerative colitis.
source: This axis represents an important resolution pathway in chronic inflammatory settings such as those of rheumatoid arthritis (D'Acquisto et al., 2008) and ulcerative colitis (Vong et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to D'Acquisto et al., 2008 and Vong et al., 2012

claim: ANXA1 belongs to the annexin family of Ca2+-dependent phospholipid-binding proteins and reduces eicosanoid production through inhibition of phospholipase A2.
source: ANXA1 belongs to the annexin family of Ca2+-dependent phospholipid-binding proteins, and through inhibition of phospholipase A2, it reduces eicosanoid production, which also contributes to its anti-inflammatory activities.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about ANXA1 function

claim: ANXA1 promotes modulation of M2 macrophage phenotype to attenuate tissue inflammation.
source: Modulation of M2 macrophage phenotype is also promoted by ANXA1 to attenuate tissue inflammation (McArthur et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to McArthur et al., 2020

claim: Corticosteroids increase the synthesis of ANXA1.
source: Corticosteroids (a mainstay of asthma treatment) increase the synthesis of ANXA1 (Rhen and Cidlowski, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rhen and Cidlowski, 2005

claim: Plasma ANXA1 levels are significantly lower in asthmatic patients with frequent exacerbations compared to those with stable disease.
source: Plasma ANXA1 levels are significantly lower in asthmatic patients with frequent exacerbations compared to those with stable disease, suggesting a link between this mediator and disease state (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2018

claim: Children with wheeze have reduced airway levels of ANXA1.
source: Furthermore, children with wheeze have reduced airway levels of ANXA1 ( Eke Gungor et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eke Gungor et al., 2014

claim: Previous studies using anxa1-/- deficient mice challenged with ovalbumin showed anxa1-deficient mice to have elevated AHR compared to WT mice.
source: Previous functional studies using anxa1-/- deficient mice challenged with ovalbumin showed anxa1-deficient mice to have elevated AHR compared to WT mice (Ng et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ng et al., 2011

claim: Untreated anxa1-deficient mice have spontaneous AHR that predisposes them to exacerbated response to allergen.
source: Ng et al. demonstrated that untreated anxa1-deficient mice have spontaneous AHR that predisposes them to exacerbated response to allergen (Ng et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ng et al., 2011

claim: Anxa1 expression was found to be characteristic of a novel cell type called the Hillock cell, which may be involved in squamous barrier function and immunomodulation.
source: Of interest, in mice, anxa1 expression was recently found to be characteristic of a novel cell type called the Hillock cell, which may be involved in squamous barrier function and immunomodulation (Montoro et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Montoro et al., 2018

claim: The ANXA1/FPR2 signalling axis is an important regulator of allergic disease that could be manipulated for therapeutic benefit.
source: These data identify the ANXA1/FPR2 signalling axis as an important regulator of allergic disease, that could be manipulated for therapeutic benefit.
evidence: Inference from the combined GWAS and functional experimental data

claim: A comparatively small GWAS using a specific subtype of early-onset childhood asthma with recurrent severe exacerbations identified a functional variant in CDHR3 (SNP rs6967330).
source: For example, a comparatively small GWAS (1173 cases and 2522 controls) which used a specific subtype of early-onset childhood asthma with recurrent severe exacerbations as an outcome identified a functional variant in a novel susceptibility gene CDHR3 (SNP rs6967330) as an associate of this disease subtype, but not of doctor-diagnosed asthma (Bønnelykke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bønnelykke et al., 2014

claim: The largest asthma GWAS to date reported no significant association between CDHR3 and aggregated asthma diagnosis despite having ~40-fold higher sample size.
source: In contrast, the largest asthma GWAS to date had an ~40-fold higher sample size (Demenais et al., 2018), but reported no significant association between CDHR3 and aggregated asthma diagnosis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Demenais et al., 2018

claim: With careful phenotyping, smaller sample sizes may be adequately powered to identify larger effect sizes than those in large GWASs with broader outcome definitions.
source: Therefore, with careful phenotyping, smaller sample sizes may be adequately powered to identify larger effect sizes than those in large GWASs with broader outcome definitions (Schoettler et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoettler et al., 2019 and inference from the CDHR3 example

claim: Previous studies in ALSPAC found that 17q21 SNPs are associated with early-onset persistent, but not with early transient or late-onset wheeze.
source: Our current findings are consistent with our earlier report suggesting that 17q21 SNPs are associated with early-onset persistent, but not with early transient or late-onset wheeze (Granell et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Granell et al., 2013

claim: The 46 highest ranked SNPs predicted persistent wheeze more strongly than doctor-diagnosed asthma in ALSPAC.
source: Further analysis using genetic prediction scores based on 10–200,000 SNPs ranked according to their associations with physician-diagnosed asthma found that the 46 highest ranked SNPs predicted persistent wheeze more strongly than doctor-diagnosed asthma (Spycher et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spycher et al., 2012

claim: A candidate gene study found different associations of IL33-IL1RL1 pathway polymorphisms with different wheeze phenotypes.
source: Finally, a candidate gene study combining data from ALSPAC and PIAMA found different associations of IL33-IL1RL1 pathway polymorphisms with different phenotypes (Savenije et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Savenije et al., 2014

claim: There is considerable heterogeneity in LCA-derived wheeze phenotypes between studies in temporal trajectories, distributions within a population, and associated risk factors.
source: However, there is a considerable heterogeneity in LCA-derived wheeze phenotypes between studies, and although phenotypes in different studies are usually designated with the same names, they differ between studies in temporal trajectories, distributions within a population, and associated risk factors (Oksel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oksel et al., 2018

claim: Heterogeneity in wheeze phenotypes is in part consequent on the number and non-uniformity of time points used and is likely one of the factors responsible for the lack of consistent associations with risk factors.
source: This heterogeneity is in part consequent on the number and the non-uniformity of the time points used, and is likely one of the factors responsible for the lack of consistent associations of discovered phenotypes with risk factors reported in previous studies (Oksel et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oksel et al., 2019b and inference

claim: Less distinct wheeze phenotypes were identified in PIAMA compared to those derived in ALSPAC.
source: For example, we have previously shown that less distinct wheeze phenotypes in PIAMA were identified compared to those derived in ALSPAC (Savenije et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Savenije et al., 2011

claim: Phenotypes that are homogeneous to those in this study almost certainly cannot readily be derived in available populations.
source: Thus, phenotypes that are homogeneous to those in our study almost certainly cannot readily be derived in available populations.
evidence: Inference from the heterogeneity of LCA-derived phenotypes across studies

claim: The number of individuals assigned to persistent wheezing in PIAMA was small, associates of this phenotype differed to those in STELAR cohorts, and the SNPs' imputation scores were low (<0.60).
source: In this analysis, the number of individuals assigned to persistent wheezing in PIAMA was small (Võsa et al., 2018), associates of this phenotype differed to those in STELAR cohorts, and the SNPs' imputation scores were low (<0.60), which meant the conditions for replication were not met.
evidence: Results from attempted replication in PIAMA cohort

claim: The study population is of European descent and results cannot be generalised to different ethnicities or environments.
source: Our study population is of European descent, and we cannot generalise the results to different ethnicities or environments.
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitation

claim: There is under-representation of ethnically diverse populations in most GWASs.
source: It is important to highlight the under-representation of ethnically diverse populations in most GWASs (Kim and Ober, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Ober, 2019

claim: Large consortia have been formed to combine results of multiple ethnically diverse GWASs to increase power to identify asthma susceptibility loci.
source: To mitigate against this, large consortia have been formed, which combine the results of multiple ethnically diverse GWASs to increase the overall power to identify asthma susceptibility loci. Examples include the GABRIEL (Moffatt et al., 2010), EVE (Torgerson et al., 2011), and TAGC (Demenais et al., 2018) consortia, and the value of diverse, multiethnic participants in large-scale genomic studies has recently been shown (Wojcik et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple consortia studies

claim: The study used data from five birth cohorts with detailed and lifelong phenotyping, which were harmonised in a common knowledge management platform.
source: One strength of our approach is that we used data from five birth cohorts with detailed and lifelong phenotyping, which were harmonised in a common knowledge management platform (Custovic et al., 2015), allowing joint analyses.
evidence: Description of study methodology with citation to Custovic et al., 2015

claim: Three parallel GWASs produced estimates with remarkably consistent directions of effects.
source: We performed three parallel GWASs that produced estimates with remarkably consistent directions of effects.
evidence: Observation from the GWAS meta-analysis results

claim: Targeting pathways to promote the clearance of chronic inflammation in persistent disease may represent an exciting therapeutic prospect.
source: Targeting these pathways to promote the clearance of chronic inflammation in persistent disease may represent an exciting therapeutic prospect.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the study findings

claim: The pro-resolving anxa1 may play a role in regulating the pulmonary immune response to allergen.
source: This increase suggests that the pro-resolving anxa1 may play a role in regulating the pulmonary immune response to allergen.
evidence: Inference from the murine model data showing anxa1 induction following HDM exposure

claim: Loss of anxa1 results in heightened airway hyperreactivity and Th2 inflammation upon allergen challenge.
source: Using anxa1-/- deficient mice, we showed that loss of anxa1 results in heightened airway hyperreactivity and Th2 inflammation upon allergen challenge.
evidence: Results from murine model experiments using anxa1-/- mice

claim: The risk allele (T) of rs75260654 confers a reduction in ANXA1 expression.
source: We identified rs75260654 as the most likely causative single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) using Promoter Capture Hi-C loops, and then showed that the risk allele (T) confers a reduction in ANXA1 expression.
evidence: Results from PCHi-C and eQTL analyses

claim: 44 independent SNPs were associated with early-onset persistent wheeze at p<10-5.
source: Forty-four independent SNPs were associated with early-onset persistent, 25 with pre-school remitting, 33 with mid-childhood remitting, and 32 with late-onset wheeze.
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis

claim: 25 independent SNPs were associated with pre-school remitting wheeze at p<10-5.
source: Forty-four independent SNPs were associated with early-onset persistent, 25 with pre-school remitting, 33 with mid-childhood remitting, and 32 with late-onset wheeze.
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis

claim: 33 independent SNPs were associated with mid-childhood remitting wheeze at p<10-5.
source: Forty-four independent SNPs were associated with early-onset persistent, 25 with pre-school remitting, 33 with mid-childhood remitting, and 32 with late-onset wheeze.
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis

claim: 32 independent SNPs were associated with late-onset wheeze at p<10-5.
source: Forty-four independent SNPs were associated with early-onset persistent, 25 with pre-school remitting, 33 with mid-childhood remitting, and 32 with late-onset wheeze.
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis

claim: A novel locus on chr9q21.13 (close to annexin 1 [ANXA1], p<6.7 × 10-9) was identified and associated exclusively with early-onset persistent wheeze.
source: We identified a novel locus on chr9q21.13 (close to annexin 1 [ANXA1], p<6.7 × 10-9), associated exclusively with early-onset persistent wheeze.
evidence: Results from the GWAS meta-analysis

claim: Genetic deletion of anxa1 potentiated the development of AHR and enhanced eosinophilia and markers of Th2 inflammation in mice treated with HDM.
source: In addition, genetic deletion of anxa1 potentiated the development of AHR and enhanced eosinophilia and markers of Th2 inflammation in mice treated with HDM, which is consistent with and extends previous reports.
evidence: Results from murine model experiments
